meta.description: Claude-generated questions that passed independent verification (blind solve, key check, computed check where a verify_code is given, duplicate check), with the trap, format and verify_code fixes already applied.

questions.concept_tag: Percentages - total from the passed share
questions.question_text: In a test, 25% of the candidates failed and 600 candidates passed. How many candidates appeared in the test?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Passed = 100% - 25% = 75% of the total. So 75% of T = 600 and T = 600 ÷ 3/4 = 800. Shortcut: 75% = 3/4, so multiply the passed number by 4/3. Trap (B): 750 comes from adding 25% of the passed number to 600, using the wrong base. Trap (C): 625 comes from adding 25 candidates to 600, as though 25% meant 25. Trap (D): 2,400 comes from treating 600 as the failed 25% (600 ÷ 1/4).

questions.concept_tag: Profit & Loss - selling price from profit percent
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper buys a bag for ₹640 and sells it at a profit of 15%. What is the selling price of the bag?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Profit = 15% of 640 = 96, so SP = 640 + 96 = ₹736. Shortcut: 640 × 1.15 = 736 in one step. Trap (A): 655 comes from adding 15 rupees to the cost, treating 15% as ₹15. Trap (B): 544 comes from multiplying by 0.85, which is the selling price at a 15% loss. Trap (D): 96 is only the profit; the cost price was not added back.

questions.concept_tag: Simple Interest - rate from principal and amount
questions.question_text: A sum of ₹4,000 becomes ₹5,000 in 5 years at simple interest. What is the rate of interest per annum?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Interest = 5,000 - 4,000 = ₹1,000 over 5 years. Rate = (1,000 × 100) / (4,000 × 5) = 5% per annum. Shortcut: 1,000 is 25% of 4,000 over 5 years, so 25 ÷ 5 = 5. Trap (A): 25 is the total interest as a percentage of the principal; the time was never divided out. Trap (C): 4 comes from using the amount ₹5,000 as the principal in the denominator: 1,000 × 100 / (5,000 × 5). Trap (D): 20 uses the amount as the principal and also forgets to divide by time.

questions.question_text: ₹7,200 is divided between P and Q in the ratio 5 : 7. How much more does Q get than P?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total parts = 5 + 7 = 12, so one part = 7,200 ÷ 12 = 600. Q gets 7 × 600 = 4,200 and P gets 5 × 600 = 3,000, so Q gets 4,200 - 3,000 = ₹1,200 more. Shortcut: (difference of ratio terms) × (one part) = 2 × 600. Trap (A): 3,000 is P's share, not the difference. Trap (B): 4,200 is Q's share, not the difference. Trap (C): 600 is one part; the ratio difference of 2 was ignored.

questions.question_text: What is 3/4 of 2/5 of 320?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 2/5 of 320 = 128, and 3/4 of 128 = 96. Shortcut: 3/4 × 2/5 = 3/10, and 3/10 of 320 = 96. Trap (A): 128 is only 2/5 of 320; the 3/4 was skipped. Trap (C): 240 is only 3/4 of 320; the 2/5 was skipped. Trap (D): 368 comes from adding the fractions (3/4 + 2/5 = 23/20) and taking that fraction of 320 instead of multiplying them.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = Fraction(3, 4) * Fraction(2, 5) * 320

questions.question_text: A can finish a piece of work in 9 days and B can finish it in 18 days. In how many days will they finish it working together?

options.D: 4.5 days

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In one day A does 1/9 and B does 1/18, together 1/9 + 1/18 = 3/18 = 1/6, so they take 6 days. Shortcut: take total work = 18 units; A = 2 units/day, B = 1 unit/day, together 3 units/day, and 18 ÷ 3 = 6. Trap (B): 13.5 is the simple average of 9 and 18; two workers together must beat the faster one. Trap (C): 27 is the sum of the two times. Trap (D): 4.5 is 9 ÷ 2, assuming both work at A's speed.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = 1 / (Fraction(1, 9) + Fraction(1, 18))

questions.concept_tag: Pipes & Cisterns - leak time from delay
questions.question_text: A tap fills a tank in 6 hours. Because of a leak at the bottom, the tank takes 8 hours to fill. In how many hours can the leak alone empty the full tank?

options.D: 24 hours

questions.trap_type: Extra time taken as leak time
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tap alone: 1/6 per hour. With the leak: 1/8 per hour. Leak rate = 1/6 - 1/8 = 1/24 per hour, so the leak alone empties the tank in 24 hours. Shortcut: take capacity = LCM(6, 8) = 24 units; tap = 4/h, net = 3/h, so the leak = 1/h and empties 24 units in 24 h. Trap (A): 2 is the extra time, 8 - 6. Trap (B): 14 adds 6 and 8. Trap (C): 48 multiplies 6 and 8.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = 1 / (Fraction(1, 6) - Fraction(1, 8))

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - trains approaching each other
questions.question_text: Two stations are 360 km apart. Two trains start from them at the same time and move towards each other at 50 km/h and 70 km/h. After how many hours do they meet?

options.D: 6 hours

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The trains approach each other, so the relative speed = 50 + 70 = 120 km/h. Time = 360 ÷ 120 = 3 hours. Shortcut: add speeds when moving towards each other, subtract when moving the same way. Trap (A): 7.2 is 360 ÷ 50, using only the slower train. Trap (B): 18 is 360 ÷ 20, subtracting speeds as if the trains moved in the same direction. Trap (D): 6 is 360 ÷ 60, using the average speed instead of the combined speed.

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - fencing cost of a square from its area
questions.question_text: The area of a square field is 1,296 m². What is the cost of fencing it at ₹15 per metre?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Side = √1,296 = 36 m. Perimeter = 4 × 36 = 144 m. Cost = 144 × 15 = ₹2,160. Shortcut: recognise 36² = 1,296, then fencing needs the perimeter (4 × side), not the area. Trap (B): 540 uses one side only (36 × 15). Trap (C): 19,440 multiplies the area by ₹15. Trap (D): 1,080 uses half the perimeter (72 × 15).
questions.verify_code:
import math
side = math.isqrt(1296)
answer = 4 * side * 15

questions.question_text: What is the value of 48 ÷ 6 × 2 + 5² - 3 × 4?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Powers first: 5² = 25. Then ÷ and × from left to right: 48 ÷ 6 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16, and 3 × 4 = 12. Finally + and -: 16 + 25 - 12 = 29. Shortcut: order is brackets, orders (powers), then division and multiplication left to right, then addition and subtraction. Trap (A): 17 comes from 48 ÷ (6 × 2) = 4, doing the multiplication before the division. Trap (B): 14 reads 5² as 10. Trap (C): 152 works strictly left to right, ignoring that × outranks + and -.

questions.concept_tag: Percentages - one quantity as a percent of another with units
questions.question_text: What percent of 1.2 kg is 300 g?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Convert to the same unit: 1.2 kg = 1,200 g. Percentage = (300 / 1,200) × 100 = 25%. Shortcut: 300 g is a quarter of 1,200 g. Trap (A): 250 divides 300 by 1.2 without converting units. Trap (B): 400 inverts the ratio (1,200 / 300 × 100). Trap (D): 2.5 over-converts, treating 1.2 kg as 12,000 g.

questions.concept_tag: Discount - marked price from selling price
questions.question_text: After a discount of 20% on its marked price, a television is sold for ₹16,000. What is its marked price?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The selling price is 80% of the marked price: 0.8 × MP = 16,000, so MP = ₹20,000. Shortcut: 80% = 4/5, so MP = 16,000 × 5/4. Trap (A): 19,200 adds 20% of the selling price (16,000 × 1.2); the discount was on the marked price, not the selling price. Trap (C): 12,800 applies the 20% discount a second time to the selling price. Trap (D): 3,200 is 20% of the selling price, which is not the marked price.

questions.question_text: What is the compound interest on ₹6,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Year 1 interest = 10% of 6,000 = 600, giving 6,600. Year 2 interest = 10% of 6,600 = 660. CI = 600 + 660 = ₹1,260. Shortcut: two successive 10% increases equal 21%, and 21% of 6,000 = 1,260. Trap (A): 1,200 is simple interest (600 a year for 2 years). Trap (B): 7,260 is the amount, not the interest. Trap (C): 1,320 doubles the second-year interest (660 × 2).
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = 6000 * (Fraction(11, 10) ** 2 - 1)

questions.concept_tag: Number System - least number to add for divisibility
questions.question_text: What is the least number that must be added to 1,000 so that the sum is exactly divisible by 24?
questions.trap_type: Used remainder instead of divisor minus remainder
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 1,000 ÷ 24 gives quotient 41 and remainder 16. The next multiple of 24 is 24 × 42 = 1,008, so the number to add is 24 - 16 = 8. Shortcut: number to add = divisor - remainder. Trap (B): 16 is the remainder itself, which is what you would subtract, not add. Trap (C): 41 is the quotient. Trap (D): 1,008 is the resulting sum, not the number to be added.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(n for n in range(24) if (1000 + n) % 24 == 0)

questions.question_text: The radius of a wheel is 35 cm. How many complete revolutions does it make to cover 220 m? (Take π = 22/7)
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm = 2.2 m. Revolutions = 220 m ÷ 2.2 m = 100. Shortcut: for r = 35 (a multiple of 7), the circumference is 220 cm, so 22,000 cm ÷ 220 cm = 100. Trap (A): 1 compares 220 m with 220 cm without converting units. Trap (B): 200 uses πr = 110 cm as the circumference. Trap (D): 10 converts 220 m into 2,200 cm, a slip of a factor of 10.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
circ_cm = 2 * Fraction(22, 7) * 35
answer = Fraction(22000) / circ_cm

questions.concept_tag: Ratio - ages from the age difference
questions.question_text: The present ages of a father and his son are in the ratio 7 : 2. If the father is 35 years older than the son, what is the father's present age?

options.D: 63 years

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The ratio is 7 : 2, so the difference is 5 parts = 35 years and one part = 7 years. Father = 7 × 7 = 49 years (the son is 14). Shortcut: father = difference × 7/5 = 35 × 7/5. Trap (A): 14 is the son's age, not the father's. Trap (C): 35 is just the age difference. Trap (D): 63 multiplies the sum of the ratio terms (9) by the part value 7.

questions.question_text: What is the value of 17² - 13²?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 17² - 13² = (17 - 13)(17 + 13) = 4 × 30 = 120. Shortcut: use a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b) instead of squaring both numbers. Trap (A): 16 squares the difference, (17 - 13)². Trap (B): 4 stops after finding the difference. Trap (D): 30 stops after finding the sum.

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - speed with time in minutes
questions.question_text: A cyclist covers 30 km in 40 minutes. What is the speed of the cyclist in km/h?

options.D: 45 km/h

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 40 minutes = 2/3 hour, so speed = 30 ÷ (2/3) = 45 km/h. Shortcut: 30 km in 40 min means in 60 min the cyclist covers 30 × 60/40 = 45 km. Trap (A): 0.75 is the speed in km per minute and was never converted to km/h. Trap (B): 75 treats 40 minutes as 0.4 hour (30 ÷ 0.4). Trap (C): 30 ignores the time and reads the distance as the hourly speed.

questions.concept_tag: Boats & Streams - still-water speed from upstream
questions.question_text: A boat takes 3 hours to go 24 km upstream. If the speed of the stream is 2 km/h, what is the speed of the boat in still water?

options.D: 12 km/h

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Upstream speed = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 km/h, which equals boat speed - stream speed. So boat speed = 8 + 2 = 10 km/h. Shortcut: still-water speed = upstream speed + stream speed. Trap (B): 8 is the upstream speed itself. Trap (C): 6 subtracts the stream (8 - 2) instead of adding it. Trap (D): 12 is the downstream speed (10 + 2), not the still-water speed.
questions.verify_code: answer = 24 // 3 + 2

questions.concept_tag: Mixtures - quantity of one component from a ratio
questions.question_text: A 40-litre mixture of milk and water has the two in the ratio 3 : 2. How many litres of milk does it contain?

options.D: 120 litres

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total parts = 3 + 2 = 5, so one part = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 litres. Milk = 3 × 8 = 24 litres. Shortcut: milk is 3/5 of the mixture, and 3/5 of 40 = 24. Trap (A): 16 is the water (2 parts), not the milk. Trap (C): 60 multiplies 40 by 3/2, treating the ratio as a scale factor on the whole mixture. Trap (D): 120 multiplies 40 by 3 without dividing by the total number of parts.

questions.concept_tag: Percentages - successive spending on changing bases
questions.question_text: A man spends 20% of his monthly income on rent and then 30% of the remaining amount on food. After these two expenses he is left with ₹5,600. What is his monthly income?
questions.trap_type: Percentage taken on the wrong base
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the income be I. After rent, 80% of I remains. Food takes 30% of that, so 70% of 0.8I remains: 0.8I × 0.7 = 0.56I = 5,600, hence I = 10,000. Shortcut: remaining fraction = 4/5 × 7/10 = 14/25, so I = 5,600 × 25/14 = 10,000. Trap (A): 11,200 treats food as 30% of the whole income (20% + 30% = 50% spent, so 0.5I = 5,600). Trap (B): 7,000 ignores the food expense and sets 0.8I = 5,600. Trap (D): 8,736 multiplies the leftover by 1.2 and then 1.3, undoing the percentages by multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.concept_tag: Profit & Loss - buying and selling both at a discount
questions.question_text: A trader buys goods at a discount of 20% on the marked price and sells them at a discount of 10% on the same marked price. What is his profit percentage?
questions.trap_type: Profit taken on the wrong base
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take the marked price as 100. Cost = 80 (20% discount) and selling price = 90 (10% discount), so profit = 10 on a cost of 80, i.e. 10/80 × 100 = 12.5%. Shortcut: profit % = (gap between the discounts) ÷ (100 − buying discount) × 100. Trap (B): 10% is the gap between the discounts read directly as a percentage, though the base is the cost, not the marked price. Trap (C): 11.1% divides the profit by the selling price (10/90). Trap (D): 90% is only the selling price as a percentage of the marked price.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
cp = Fraction(80)
sp = Fraction(90)
answer = (sp - cp) / cp * 100

questions.concept_tag: Simple Interest - principal from two amounts
questions.question_text: A sum of money at simple interest amounts to ₹1,260 in 2 years and to ₹1,440 in 4 years. What is the sum?
questions.trap_type: Subtracted the wrong amount of interest
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Simple interest is the same every year. Between year 2 and year 4 the amount rises by 1,440 − 1,260 = 180, so 2 years of interest = 180, i.e. ₹90 per year. Principal = amount after 2 years − interest for 2 years = 1,260 − 180 = ₹1,080. Shortcut: principal = A₂ − 2 × (yearly interest). Trap (A): 1,170 subtracts only one year's interest (90) from 1,260. Trap (B): 900 reads 180 as a single year's interest and subtracts 2 × 180 = 360. Trap (C): 1,350 takes the average of the two amounts as the principal.
questions.verify_code:
yearly = (1440 - 1260) // 2
answer = 1260 - 2 * yearly

questions.question_text: The average marks of 40 students were calculated as 72. Later it was found that one student's mark had been entered as 96 instead of 69, and another student's mark as 45 instead of 54. What is the correct average?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Wrong total = 40 × 72 = 2,880. The first correction lowers the total by 96 − 69 = 27, the second raises it by 54 − 45 = 9, so the net change is −18 and the correct total = 2,862. Correct average = 2,862 ÷ 40 = 71.55. Shortcut: the average moves by (net error) ÷ 40 = −18/40 = −0.45, so 72 − 0.45 = 71.55. Trap (A): 72.45 gets the direction of the net correction wrong (+0.45). Trap (C): 71.325 corrects only the first entry (−27/40 = −0.675). Trap (D): 71.1 adds the two error sizes (27 + 9 = 36) as if both lowered the total (−0.9).
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = Fraction(40 * 72 - 27 + 9, 40)

questions.concept_tag: Time & Work - whole-job days from part-job data
questions.question_text: A can do 1/3 of a piece of work in 5 days and B can do 2/5 of the same work in 10 days. In how many days can they finish the whole work together?

options.D: 40 days

questions.trap_type: Part of a job treated as the whole job
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A alone: 5 ÷ (1/3) = 15 days. B alone: 10 ÷ (2/5) = 25 days. Together they do 1/15 + 1/25 = 5/75 + 3/75 = 8/75 of the work per day, so the whole work takes 75/8 = 9.375 days. Shortcut: take total work = 75 units; A does 5 units a day, B does 3, together 8 units a day. Trap (A): 3.33 treats the partial jobs as complete jobs (5 and 10 days), giving 1/(1/5 + 1/10) = 10/3. Trap (C): 20 is the average of 15 and 25; working together must beat the faster worker. Trap (D): 40 adds 15 and 25.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
a = Fraction(5) / Fraction(1, 3)
b = Fraction(10) / Fraction(2, 5)
answer = 1 / (1 / a + 1 / b)

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - train length from platform and pole times
questions.question_text: A train takes 30 seconds to cross a platform 300 m long and 20 seconds to cross a pole standing on the platform. What is the length of the train?
questions.trap_type: Train length ignored in platform crossing
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The only difference between the two crossings is the platform: the extra 30 − 20 = 10 seconds are spent covering 300 m. So speed = 300 ÷ 10 = 30 m/s. Crossing the pole means covering the train's own length in 20 seconds, so length = 30 × 20 = 600 m. Check: train + platform = 900 m = 30 m/s × 30 s. Shortcut: speed = platform length ÷ (difference of the two times). Trap (A): 900 m is the distance covered while crossing the platform (train + platform), not the train. Trap (B): 300 m is just the platform length. Trap (D): 200 m uses speed = 300 ÷ 30 = 10 m/s, forgetting that the train must also clear its own length.
questions.verify_code:
speed = 300 // (30 - 20)
answer = speed * 20

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - recasting a sphere into cones
questions.question_text: A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into small solid cones, each of base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. How many cones are obtained?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Volume is conserved. Sphere = (4/3)π(6)³ = 288π. Cone = (1/3)π(3)²(4) = 12π. Number of cones = 288π ÷ 12π = 24. Shortcut: π cancels, so compute (4/3 × 216) ÷ (1/3 × 9 × 4) = 288 ÷ 12. Trap (A): 8 uses the cone volume without the 1/3 factor (36π), giving 288 ÷ 36. Trap (B): 18 uses the sphere volume without the 4/3 factor (216π ÷ 12π). Trap (C): 192 takes the diameter 12 cm as the radius of the sphere, giving (4/3)(12)³ = 2,304 and 2,304 ÷ 12.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
sphere = Fraction(4, 3) * 6 ** 3
cone = Fraction(1, 3) * 3 ** 2 * 4
answer = sphere / cone

questions.question_text: What is the value of 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + 1/2))?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Work from the innermost bracket outwards. 1 + 1/2 = 3/2. Then 1/(3/2) = 2/3, so the next bracket is 1 + 2/3 = 5/3. Then 1/(5/3) = 3/5, so the whole expression is 1 + 3/5 = 8/5. Shortcut: at each level flip the previous result and add 1 (3/2 → 5/3 → 8/5). Trap (B): 5/8 inverts the final answer instead of adding it to 1. Trap (C): 5/3 stops after the second level and misses the outermost 1 + 1/(...). Trap (D): 3/2 stops after the innermost bracket.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
inner = 1 + Fraction(1, 2)
mid = 1 + 1 / inner
answer = 1 + 1 / mid

questions.concept_tag: Percentages - comparing two quantities through a third
questions.question_text: A's salary is 20% less than B's salary, and C's salary is 25% more than B's salary. By what percentage is C's salary more than A's salary?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take B = 100. Then A = 80 and C = 125. C exceeds A by 45, and the base is A (the salary being compared with), so the excess is 45/80 × 100 = 56.25%. Shortcut: C/A = 1.25/0.8 = 25/16, so C is 9/16 = 56.25% more than A. Trap (A): 45% reads the gap of 45 (or 20 + 25) directly as a percentage. Trap (B): 36% divides the gap by C (45/125) instead of by A. Trap (D): 5% subtracts the two percentages (25 − 20).
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
a = Fraction(4, 5)
c = Fraction(5, 4)
answer = (c - a) / a * 100

questions.concept_tag: Ratio - income, expenditure and equal savings
questions.question_text: The incomes of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 4 and their expenditures are in the ratio 3 : 2. If each of them saves ₹1,600, what is A's income?
questions.trap_type: Savings taken as one ratio part
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the incomes be 5x and 4x and the expenditures 3k and 2k. Savings: 5x − 3k = 1,600 and 4x − 2k = 1,600. Multiply the second equation by 3/2 to get 6x − 3k = 2,400, then subtract the first equation: x = 800. So A's income = 5 × 800 = ₹4,000 (k = 800, so A spends 2,400, B earns 3,200 and spends 1,600). Shortcut: scale one equation so the expenditure terms match, then subtract. Trap (A): ₹3,200 is B's income. Trap (B): ₹2,400 is A's expenditure. Trap (C): ₹8,000 treats the savings as one ratio part and multiplies 5 × 1,600.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(5 * x for x in range(1, 1001) for k in range(1, 1001) if 5 * x - 3 * k == 1600 and 4 * x - 2 * k == 1600)

questions.concept_tag: Simple Interest - splitting a sum between two rates
questions.question_text: ₹6,000 is lent in two parts, one at 5% and the other at 8% simple interest per annum. The total interest for one year is ₹405. What is the sum lent at 5%?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Mean rate = 405/6,000 = 6.75%. By alligation, (amount at 5%) : (amount at 8%) = (8 − 6.75) : (6.75 − 5) = 1.25 : 1.75 = 5 : 7. So the part at 5% = 5/12 × 6,000 = ₹2,500. Check: 2,500 × 5% = 125 and 3,500 × 8% = 280, total 405. Shortcut: the mean rate lies closer to the rate that carries more money, so the amount at 5% is the smaller part. Trap (A): 3,500 reverses the alligation ratio and gives the amount at 8%. Trap (C): 3,000 assumes the sum is split equally. Trap (D): 3,750 takes 5/8 of 6,000, using the wrong total (8) for the ratio 5 : 7.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(x for x in range(0, 6001) if 5 * x + 8 * (6000 - x) == 40500)

questions.concept_tag: Profit & Loss - profit given as a percentage of selling price
questions.question_text: On an article, the profit is 20% of its selling price. What is the profit percentage on its cost price?
questions.trap_type: Profit taken on the wrong base
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take SP = 100. Profit = 20, so CP = 100 − 20 = 80. Profit on cost = 20/80 × 100 = 25%. Shortcut: if profit is p% of SP, profit on cost = p/(100 − p) × 100 = 20/80 × 100. Trap (A): 20% reads the given percentage as profit on cost, but the stated base is the selling price. Trap (B): 80% is the cost price as a percentage of the selling price. Trap (D): 125% is the selling price as a percentage of the cost price, not the profit.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
sp = Fraction(100)
profit = Fraction(20)
cp = sp - profit
answer = profit / cp * 100

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - chase with a head start
questions.question_text: A policeman sees a thief 100 m ahead of him. The thief runs at 8 m/s and the policeman chases at 10 m/s. How far does the thief run before being caught?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The policeman gains 10 − 8 = 2 m every second, so closing the 100 m gap takes 100 ÷ 2 = 50 s. In that time the thief runs 8 × 50 = 400 m. Check: the policeman runs 10 × 50 = 500 m = 400 m + 100 m head start. Shortcut: thief's distance = gap × (thief's speed) ÷ (difference of speeds) = 100 × 8 ÷ 2. Trap (B): 500 m is the distance run by the policeman. Trap (C): 800 m multiplies the gap by the thief's speed (100 × 8) and forgets to divide by the speed difference. Trap (D): 50 is the time in seconds, not a distance.
questions.verify_code:
gap = 100
time = gap // (10 - 8)
answer = 8 * time

questions.concept_tag: Number System - largest n-digit multiple of several numbers
questions.question_text: What is the largest 4-digit number that is exactly divisible by 15, 18 and 24?
questions.trap_type: Used the LCM of only two of the numbers
questions.pedagogical_explanation: LCM: 15 = 3 × 5, 18 = 2 × 3², 24 = 2³ × 3, so LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360. The largest 4-digit number is 9,999; 9,999 ÷ 360 leaves remainder 279, so the answer is 9,999 − 279 = 9,720 (= 27 × 360). Shortcut: largest n-digit number minus its remainder on division by the LCM. Trap (A): 9,360 steps back one multiple of 360 too many (26 × 360). Trap (C): 9,990 is the answer for 15 and 18 only (LCM 90); it is not divisible by 24. Trap (D): 10,080 is the next multiple of 360, which has 5 digits.
questions.verify_code: answer = max(n for n in range(1000, 10000) if n % 15 == 0 and n % 18 == 0 and n % 24 == 0)

questions.concept_tag: Number System - remainder under a smaller divisor
questions.question_text: A number leaves a remainder of 29 when divided by 56. What is the remainder when the same number is divided by 8?
questions.trap_type: Assumed the remainder stays the same
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Write the number as N = 56k + 29. Since 8 divides 56, the part 56k is a multiple of 8, so the remainder on division by 8 is the remainder of 29 on division by 8, which is 5 (29 = 3 × 8 + 5). Shortcut: when the new divisor is a factor of the old one, reduce the old remainder by the new divisor. Trap (A): 29 assumes the remainder is unchanged, but a remainder must be smaller than the divisor 8. Trap (B): 1 divides by 7 (the other factor of 56) instead of 8. Trap (C): 0 assumes N is divisible by 8 just because 8 divides 56, ignoring the leftover 29.
questions.verify_code:
n = 56 * 5 + 29
answer = n % 8

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - area of a path around a rectangle
questions.question_text: A rectangular park is 60 m long and 40 m wide. A path 2.5 m wide runs all around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The path is outside, so the outer rectangle is (60 + 2 × 2.5) by (40 + 2 × 2.5) = 65 m by 45 m, with area 2,925 m². The park is 60 × 40 = 2,400 m². Path = 2,925 − 2,400 = 525 m². Shortcut: path area = 2w(l + b + 2w) = 5 × (100 + 5) = 525. Trap (B): 500 multiplies the park's perimeter by the width (200 × 2.5) and misses the four corner squares of 2.5 × 2.5. Trap (C): 475 treats the path as running inside the park (2,400 − 55 × 35). Trap (D): 2,925 stops at the area of the outer rectangle.

questions.question_text: The population of a town increases by 10% every year. If its present population is 53,240, what was its population 3 years ago?
questions.trap_type: Applied a decrease instead of dividing by the growth factor
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Three years of 10% growth multiply the population by 1.1³ = 1.331. So P × 1.331 = 53,240 and P = 53,240 ÷ 1.331 = 40,000. Shortcut: 1.331 = 1,331/1,000 and 53,240 = 40 × 1,331, so P = 40 × 1,000. Trap (A): 37,268 takes 30% off the present figure (53,240 × 0.7). Trap (C): 38,812 reduces by 10% three times in a row (53,240 × 0.9³), but a 10% fall does not undo a 10% rise. Trap (D): 40,954 divides by 1.3, treating three years of growth as a simple 30%.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = Fraction(53240) / Fraction(11, 10) ** 3

questions.question_text: What is the amount on ₹16,000 for 1 year at 20% per annum, compounded half-yearly?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Half-yearly compounding halves the rate and doubles the number of periods: rate = 10% per half-year, periods = 2. Amount = 16,000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = ₹19,360. Shortcut: two successive 10% rises equal a 21% rise, so 16,000 × 1.21. Trap (A): 19,200 compounds annually for 1 year (16,000 × 1.2). Trap (B): 17,600 applies only one half-year period (16,000 × 1.1). Trap (C): 23,040 uses the full 20% in each of the two half-years (16,000 × 1.2²).
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = 16000 * Fraction(11, 10) ** 2

questions.concept_tag: Number System - factor needed to make a perfect cube
questions.question_text: What is the smallest number by which 1,512 must be multiplied so that the product is a perfect cube?
questions.trap_type: Whole cube instead of the missing power
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Factorise: 1,512 = 8 × 189 = 2³ × 3³ × 7. A perfect cube needs every prime exponent to be a multiple of 3. The primes 2 and 3 already have exponent 3, but 7 has exponent 1, so two more 7s are needed: multiply by 7² = 49. The product is 74,088 = 42³. Shortcut: prime-factorise, then for each prime with exponent e (not a multiple of 3) multiply by that prime to the power (3 − e mod 3). Trap (A): 7 supplies only one more factor of 7, giving 7² in the product, which is still not a cube. Trap (B): 343 = 7³ multiplies by a whole cube of 7 instead of the missing 7². Trap (D): 189 is what is left of 1,512 after removing the cube 2³; it is not the missing factor.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(m for m in range(1, 1000) if any(k ** 3 == 1512 * m for k in range(1, 200)))

questions.concept_tag: Time & Work - wages in proportion to work done
questions.question_text: A can finish a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. With the help of C they finish it in 5 days and are paid ₹3,000 in all, shared in proportion to the work each did. What is C's share?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A and B together do 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 of the job per day. All three finish in 5 days, so the combined rate is 1/5 per day and C's rate = 1/5 - 1/6 = 1/30. In 5 days C does 5/30 = 1/6 of the whole job, so C's share = 3,000 ÷ 6 = ₹500. Shortcut: the rates are in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 (1/10 : 1/15 : 1/30 = 3/30 : 2/30 : 1/30), and since they all worked the same 5 days, the pay splits 3 : 2 : 1, so C gets 1/6. Trap (B): ₹1,000 splits the money equally among three people. Trap (C): ₹600 takes the combined rate 1/5 as C's work, so C gets 1/5 of the pay. Trap (D): ₹1,500 is A's share (A did half the job), not C's.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
a = Fraction(1, 10)
b = Fraction(1, 15)
total = Fraction(1, 5)
c = total - a - b
answer = 3000 * c / total

questions.concept_tag: Boats & Streams - distance from the two journey times
questions.question_text: A boat takes 4 hours to go a certain distance downstream and 6 hours to return the same distance upstream. If the speed of the stream is 3 km/h, what is the distance?

options.D: 60 km

questions.trap_type: Stream speed used once instead of twice
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Downstream speed = D/4 and upstream speed = D/6. Their difference is twice the stream speed: D/4 - D/6 = 2 × 3 = 6, so D/12 = 6 and D = 72 km. Check: downstream 18 km/h, upstream 12 km/h, boat 15 km/h, stream 3 km/h. Shortcut: downstream speed - upstream speed = 2 × stream speed. Trap (A): 36 sets D/4 - D/6 = 3, using the stream speed once instead of twice. Trap (C): 144 is the length of the round trip (72 + 72). Trap (D): 60 multiplies the still-water speed 15 km/h by the downstream time 4 h.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(D for D in range(1, 500) if 3 * D - 2 * D == 72)

questions.question_text: In a committee, a member aged 58 is replaced by a new member aged 28, and the average age of the committee falls by 2 years. How many members are there in the committee?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The replacement lowers the total age by 58 - 28 = 30 years. The average falls by 2, so n × 2 = 30 and n = 15. Shortcut: number of members = (change in total) ÷ (change in average). Trap (A): 60 multiplies 30 × 2 instead of dividing. Trap (B): 16 counts the new member as an extra person (15 + 1), though he only replaced someone. Trap (D): 43 averages the two ages, (58 + 28) ÷ 2, instead of using their difference.

questions.question_text: If x = √3 + √2, what is the value of x² + 1/x²?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Since (√3 + √2)(√3 - √2) = 3 - 2 = 1, we get 1/x = √3 - √2. Then x + 1/x = 2√3 and (x + 1/x)² = 12. So x² + 1/x² = 12 - 2 = 10. Direct check: x² = 5 + 2√6 and 1/x² = 5 - 2√6, which add to 10. Shortcut: x² + 1/x² = (x + 1/x)² - 2. Trap (A): 12 stops at (x + 1/x)² and forgets to subtract 2. Trap (B): 5 keeps only the rational part of x² and never adds 1/x². Trap (C): 14 adds 2 instead of subtracting it.
questions.verify_code:
import math
x = math.sqrt(3) + math.sqrt(2)
answer = round(x * x + 1 / (x * x), 6)

questions.concept_tag: Geometry - angle between two angle bisectors
questions.question_text: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 70°. The bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at the point O. What is the measure of ∠BOC?
questions.trap_type: Wrong sign in the bisector formula
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ∠B + ∠C = 180° - 70° = 110°. The bisectors give ∠OBC + ∠OCB = 110° ÷ 2 = 55°. In triangle BOC, ∠BOC = 180° - 55° = 125°. Shortcut: the angle between two internal bisectors is 90° + (third angle)/2 = 90° + 35° = 125°. Trap (B): 110° is ∠B + ∠C, before halving. Trap (C): 55° is ∠OBC + ∠OCB, which was never subtracted from 180°. Trap (D): 145° subtracts half of ∠A (35°) from 180° (180° - 35°) instead of using the 55° half-sum of ∠B and ∠C.
questions.verify_code: answer = 90 + 70 // 2

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - cylinder volume after changing radius and height
questions.question_text: The radius of a cylinder is increased by 20% and its height is decreased by 25%. By what percent does its volume change?

options.D: 19% increase

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Volume = πr²h. New volume factor = (1.2)² × 0.75 = 1.44 × 0.75 = 1.08, so the volume rises by 8%. Shortcut: 6/5 × 6/5 × 3/4 = 27/25 = 1.08. Trap (A): 5% decrease adds the percentages directly (+20 - 25 = -5). Trap (B): 10% decrease forgets that r is squared (1.2 × 0.75 = 0.9). Trap (D): 19% increase adds the squared effect of r as 44% and then subtracts 25% (44 - 25 = 19) instead of multiplying the factors.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
v = Fraction(6, 5) ** 2 * Fraction(3, 4)
answer = (v - 1) * 100

questions.concept_tag: Simple Interest - time to reach a larger multiple
questions.question_text: A sum of money becomes 3 times itself in 12 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become 5 times itself at the same rate?

options.D: 24 years

questions.trap_type: Amount multiple used instead of interest multiple
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Becoming 3 times means the interest is 2P (amount 3P minus principal P), earned in 12 years, so the interest per P of principal takes 6 years. Becoming 5 times needs interest 4P, which takes 4 × 6 = 24 years. Shortcut: time ∝ (multiple - 1), so 12 × (5 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 24. Trap (A): 20 scales the time with the amounts (12 × 5/3). Trap (B): 30 uses the interest multiple as 5P instead of 4P (12 × 5/2). Trap (C): 36 multiplies the time by 3 (12 × 3).

questions.concept_tag: Number System - digit sum of a number and its reverse
questions.question_text: The sum of a two-digit number and the number formed by reversing its digits is 143. If the tens digit is 3 more than the units digit, what is the number?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: For digits a (tens) and b (units): (10a + b) + (10b + a) = 11(a + b) = 143, so a + b = 13. With a - b = 3, a = 8 and b = 5, so the number is 85 (and 85 + 58 = 143). Shortcut: the sum of a number and its reverse is always 11 × (digit sum), so divide 143 by 11 first. Trap (A): 58 has the right digit sum but the tens digit is smaller, so it is the reversed number. Trap (C): 94 has digit sum 13 but the digits differ by 5, not 3. Trap (D): 76 has digit sum 13 but the digits differ by 1, not 3.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(n for n in range(10, 100) if n + (n % 10) * 10 + n // 10 == 143 and n // 10 - n % 10 == 3)

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - mixed modes of travel
questions.question_text: A man covers a journey of 84 km in 6 hours, partly by bus at 30 km/h and the rest on foot at 6 km/h. For how long does he walk?

options.D: 14 hours

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let him walk for t hours, so he rides for 6 - t hours: 30(6 - t) + 6t = 84, which gives 180 - 24t = 84 and t = 4 hours. Shortcut (assume all by bus): 6 h × 30 km/h = 180 km, which is 96 km too much; each hour of walking instead of riding cuts 24 km, so he walked 96 ÷ 24 = 4 hours. Trap (B): 2 hours is the time spent on the bus, not on foot. Trap (C): 3 hours assumes the time is split equally, but then the distance would be 108 km. Trap (D): 14 hours is the time for the whole 84 km on foot (84 ÷ 6).
questions.verify_code: answer = next(t for t in range(0, 7) if 30 * (6 - t) + 6 * t == 84)

questions.concept_tag: LCM - events repeating together within a time window
questions.question_text: Three bells ring at intervals of 12, 15 and 20 minutes. They ring together at 8:00 a.m. How many times do they ring together between 8:00 a.m. and 12:00 noon, counting both the 8:00 a.m. ring and the 12:00 noon ring?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The bells ring together every LCM(12, 15, 20) = 60 minutes. From 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 noon is 240 minutes, i.e. 240 ÷ 60 = 4 intervals. The rings together are at 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 o'clock, which is 5 times. Shortcut: number of simultaneous rings = (window ÷ LCM) + 1 when both end points count. Trap (A): 4 leaves out the 8:00 a.m. ring. Trap (B): 20 counts the rings of the 12-minute bell alone (240 ÷ 12). Trap (C): 6 counts both end rings on top of the 4 intervals (4 + 2), but 4 intervals give only 4 + 1 = 5 rings.
questions.verify_code:
L = next(m for m in range(1, 1000) if m % 12 == 0 and m % 15 == 0 and m % 20 == 0)
answer = 240 // L + 1

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - canvas length for a conical tent
questions.question_text: What length of canvas, 2 m wide, is needed to make a conical tent of base radius 7 m and height 24 m? (Take π = 22/7)
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Slant height l = √(7² + 24²) = √625 = 25 m. Canvas area = curved surface area = πrl = 22/7 × 7 × 25 = 550 m². Length of canvas = area ÷ width = 550 ÷ 2 = 275 m. Shortcut: recognise the 7-24-25 triple, then divide the CSA by the canvas width. Trap (A): 264 uses the height 24 m as the slant height (22/7 × 7 × 24 ÷ 2). Trap (C): 550 is the area, not divided by the width. Trap (D): 1,100 multiplies the area by the width (550 × 2) instead of dividing.
questions.verify_code:
import math
from fractions import Fraction
slant = math.isqrt(7 * 7 + 24 * 24)
answer = Fraction(22, 7) * 7 * slant / 2

questions.question_text: What is the value of √(6 + √(6 + √(6 + ...))), continuing indefinitely?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the value be x. The expression repeats inside itself, so x = √(6 + x), which gives x² = x + 6, i.e. x² - x - 6 = 0 or (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0. A square root cannot be negative, so x = 3. Shortcut: x² - x = 6 = 3 × 2, so x = 3 (the larger of two consecutive numbers whose product is 6). Trap (A): -2 is the other root of the quadratic, which a square root can never equal. Trap (B): 6 takes only the number under the first root sign. Trap (D): 2.45 is √6, the first layer only, ignoring the remaining nested layers.
questions.verify_code:
import math
x = 0.0
for i in range(60):
    x = math.sqrt(6 + x)
answer = round(x, 6)

questions.concept_tag: Time & Work - three workers from pair rates
questions.question_text: A and B together can do a piece of work in 12 days, B and C together in 15 days, and C and A together in 20 days. In how many days can all three together finish it?

options.D: 47 days

questions.trap_type: Forgot to halve the combined rate
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Adding the three pair rates counts each worker twice: 2(A + B + C) = 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/20 = 5/60 + 4/60 + 3/60 = 12/60 = 1/5. So A + B + C = 1/10 per day and all three finish in 10 days. Shortcut: take total work = 60 units; pair rates are 5, 4, 3 units a day, which total 12 and halve to 6, so 60 ÷ 6 = 10. Trap (B): 5 days uses 1/5 as the rate of all three without halving. Trap (C): 15 days just picks the middle value of the three given times. Trap (D): 47 days adds the three given times (12 + 15 + 20).
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
s = Fraction(1, 12) + Fraction(1, 15) + Fraction(1, 20)
answer = 2 / s

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - reduced speed and delay
questions.question_text: A man walks at 4/5 of his usual speed and reaches his office 20 minutes late. What is his usual time to reach the office?

options.D: 16 minutes

questions.trap_type: Answered the time on the slow day
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Speed and time are inversely proportional: at 4/5 of the speed he takes 5/4 of the time. If the usual time is t, the new time is 5t/4, and the delay is 5t/4 - t = t/4 = 20, so t = 80 minutes. Shortcut: usual time = delay ÷ (5/4 - 1) = delay × 4, because the delay is one quarter of the usual time. Trap (A): 100 minutes is the time taken on the slow day (80 + 20), not the usual time. Trap (B): 25 multiplies the delay by 5/4. Trap (D): 16 multiplies the delay by 4/5, using the speed ratio instead of the time ratio.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(t for t in range(1, 500) if 5 * t == 4 * (t + 20))

questions.concept_tag: Averages - overlapping groups and the shared item
questions.question_text: The average of 11 results is 50. The average of the first 6 results is 49 and the average of the last 6 results is 52. What is the sixth result?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sixth result belongs to both groups. Sum of first 6 = 6 × 49 = 294 and sum of last 6 = 6 × 52 = 312. Adding them counts the sixth result twice, so 294 + 312 = (sum of all 11) + (sixth result) = 550 + sixth. Hence the sixth result = 606 - 550 = 56. Shortcut: sixth = (sum of the two group totals) - (total of all). Trap (A): 50.5 is the average of the two averages (49 and 52). Trap (B): 52 assumes the sixth result equals the average of the last six. Trap (C): 49 assumes it equals the average of the first six.

questions.concept_tag: Profit & Loss - cost price from a change in selling price
questions.question_text: An article is sold at a loss of 10%. If it had been sold for ₹210 more, there would have been a profit of 5%. What is the cost price of the article?
questions.trap_type: Percentage gap read as a single percentage
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A loss of 10% means SP = 0.90 C, and a profit of 5% means SP = 1.05 C. The extra ₹210 covers the gap between them: 1.05C - 0.90C = 0.15C = 210, so C = ₹1,400. Check: SP at the loss = 1,260 and 1,260 + 210 = 1,470 = 1.05 × 1,400. Shortcut: the gap is 10% + 5% = 15% of the cost price. Trap (A): ₹4,200 divides 210 by 5% only. Trap (C): ₹2,100 divides 210 by 10% only. Trap (D): ₹1,260 is the selling price at the 10% loss, not the cost price.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(c for c in range(1, 10001) if 90 * c + 21000 == 105 * c)

questions.concept_tag: Number System - unit digit of a product of powers
questions.question_text: What is the unit digit of 6374^1793 × 625^317 × 341^491?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Only unit digits matter. 6374^1793 ends in 4^(odd) = 4 (the powers of 4 alternate 4, 6). 625^317 ends in 5. 341^491 ends in 1. The product's unit digit comes from 4 × 5 × 1 = 20, which ends in 0. Shortcut: any number ending in 5 times an even number ends in 0. Trap (A): 4 is the unit digit of the first factor alone. Trap (B): 5 is the unit digit of the second factor alone. Trap (C): 1 is the unit digit of the third factor alone.

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - wire bent from a square into a circle
questions.question_text: A wire in the form of a square of side 22 cm is bent into a circle. What is the area of the circle? (Take π = 22/7)
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The wire's length stays the same, so the circumference of the circle equals the perimeter of the square: 2πr = 4 × 22 = 88 cm, giving r = 88 × 7 ÷ 44 = 14 cm. Area = πr² = 22/7 × 14 × 14 = 616 cm². Shortcut: when the perimeter is a multiple of 44, r is a multiple of 7; here 88/44 = 2, so r = 14. Trap (B): 484 is the area of the square (22²), assuming the area stays the same. Trap (C): 154 uses r = 7, halving the radius once too often. Trap (D): 2,464 uses r = 28, which is the diameter (88 ÷ π).
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
pi = Fraction(22, 7)
r = Fraction(4 * 22) / (2 * pi)
answer = pi * r * r

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - trains after meeting
questions.question_text: Two trains start at the same time from stations A and B towards each other. After meeting, the train from A takes 4 hours to reach B and the train from B takes 9 hours to reach A. What is the ratio of the speed of the train from A to the speed of the train from B?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the speeds be a (train from A) and b (train from B), and let T be the time to meeting. After meeting, A's train covers the distance b × T that B's train covered before meeting, so bT = 4a. Similarly aT = 9b. Multiplying gives abT² = 36ab, so T = 6 hours. Then a/b = 9/T = 9/6 = 3/2. Shortcut: speed ratio = √(time of B's train after meeting ÷ time of A's train after meeting) = √(9/4) = 3/2. Trap (A): 9 : 4 is the time ratio without the square root. Trap (C): 2 : 3 is the reversed ratio (the speed of the train from B to the speed of the train from A). Trap (D): 4 : 9 uses the times directly as the speeds.
questions.verify_code:
import math
answer = math.isqrt(9)

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Write each term as a difference: 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n - 1/(n+1). The sum becomes (1 - 1/2) + (1/2 - 1/3) + ... + (1/9 - 1/10) = 1 - 1/10 = 9/10, because every middle term cancels. Shortcut: for n terms of this form the sum is n/(n+1); here n = 9. Trap (A): 1 assumes the series telescopes all the way to 1 (the infinite sum), forgetting the last 1/10. Trap (B): 10/11 counts one extra term (up to 1/(10×11)). Trap (D): 8/9 counts one term too few (up to 1/(8×9)).
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = sum(Fraction(1, n * (n + 1)) for n in range(1, 10))

questions.question_text: In a certain code language, MASTER is written as AMTSRE. How will PLANET be written in that code?

options.D: PALENT

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Compare MASTER with AMTSRE: the word splits into pairs MA, ST, ER and each pair is swapped to give AM, TS, RE. Apply the same rule to PLANET: PL, AN, ET become LP, NA, TE, so the code is LPNATE. Shortcut: split the word into pairs and test one swap against the given example before applying it. Trap (A): TENALP reverses the whole word; this fails on the example, because MASTER reversed is RETSAM, not AMTSRE. Trap (C): LPANET swaps only the first pair and leaves the rest unchanged. Trap (D): PALENT swaps the 2nd with the 3rd and the 4th with the 5th letters, pairing from the wrong starting point.
questions.verify_code:
w = 'PLANET'
answer = ''.join(w[i + 1] + w[i] for i in range(0, len(w), 2))

questions.concept_tag: Number series - perfect square plus one
questions.question_text: Find the next number in the series: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each term is one more than a perfect square: 1²+1 = 2, 2²+1 = 5, 3²+1 = 10, 4²+1 = 17, 5²+1 = 26, so the next term is 6²+1 = 37. The gaps 3, 5, 7, 9 confirm it, and the next gap is 11 (26 + 11 = 37). Shortcut: when terms are close to 4, 9, 16, 25, test 'square plus a constant'. Trap (A): 35 repeats the last gap of 9 (26 + 9). Trap (B): 36 is 6² without the +1. Trap (C): 38 raises the gap by 3 (12) instead of by 2 (11).
questions.verify_code:
seq = [n * n + 1 for n in range(1, 7)]
answer = seq[-1]

questions.concept_tag: Blood relations - spouse of an aunt
questions.question_text: Rina says to Mohan, 'Your mother's brother is the father of my son.' How is Rina's husband related to Mohan?

options.D: Mother's father

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The father of Rina's son is Rina's husband. Rina says this person is Mohan's mother's brother, so Rina's husband is Mohan's mother's brother, that is, his maternal uncle. Shortcut: replace each phrase by the person it names, 'father of my son' means 'my husband', and then read the remaining relation. Trap (A): Father comes from reading 'father of my son' as 'Mohan's father'. Trap (B): Paternal uncle picks the father's side, but the relation runs through Mohan's mother. Trap (D): Mother's father mixes up 'mother's brother' with 'mother's father'.

questions.concept_tag: Direction sense - distance from two perpendicular positions
questions.question_text: Point A is 6 m due north of point B, and point C is 8 m due east of point B. What is the shortest distance between A and C?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: North and east are at right angles, so A, B and C form a right triangle with the right angle at B. The shortest distance AC is the hypotenuse: √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 m. Shortcut: 6-8-10 is a multiple of the 3-4-5 triple. Trap (B): 14 m adds the two legs, which is the distance along the two roads, not the shortest distance. Trap (C): 2 m subtracts the legs, as if both points lay on one line. Trap (D): 48 m multiplies the legs.
questions.verify_code:
import math
answer = math.isqrt(6 * 6 + 8 * 8)

questions.question_text:
Statements: All mugs are cups. Some cups are plates. No plate is a bowl.
Conclusions:
I. Some cups are not bowls.
II. No mug is a bowl.

options.D: Both I and II follow

questions.trap_type: Property passed to the wrong set
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The cups that are plates cannot be bowls, since no plate is a bowl, so some cups are not bowls: Conclusion I follows. Nothing connects mugs to those plates, so some mugs could still be bowls; Conclusion II is not certain. Shortcut: a 'No' statement passes on to the 'Some' group it touches, but never to the larger set the 'Some' group belongs to. Trap (A): rejecting I because 'some' and 'no' cannot join into a conclusion; they can, giving 'some are not'. Trap (B): picking II alone treats all mugs as if they were the cups that are plates. Trap (D): accepting II as well, for the same reason.

questions.concept_tag: Ordering - position after two people interchange places
questions.question_text: In a row of boys, Ravi is 8th from the left end and Sunil is 12th from the right end. After they interchange their positions, Ravi becomes 20th from the left end. How many boys are there in the row?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: After the interchange, Ravi stands where Sunil stood. So Sunil's original place is 20th from the left and 12th from the right. Total = 20 + 12 - 1 = 31, because that boy is counted in both numbers. Shortcut: total = (position from left) + (position from right) - 1 for the same person. Trap (A): 32 adds 20 and 12 without subtracting the person counted twice. Trap (B): 30 subtracts 2 instead of 1. Trap (C): 19 uses Ravi's old position 8 (8 + 12 - 1) instead of his new one.
questions.verify_code: answer = 20 + 12 - 1

questions.concept_tag: Seating - linear arrangement with one elimination clue
questions.question_text: Five friends Asha, Bhanu, Charu, Deepak and Esha sit in a row facing north. Charu sits at the extreme left end. Esha sits immediately to the right of Charu. Deepak sits immediately to the left of Asha. Bhanu does not sit at the right end. Who sits in the middle?

options.D: Cannot be determined

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Place the fixed seats first: Charu is in seat 1 and Esha in seat 2. Deepak and Asha must be a side-by-side pair, Deepak on the left, in seats 3-4 or 4-5. If they take seats 3-4, Bhanu must take seat 5, which is not allowed. So Deepak is in seat 4, Asha in seat 5 and Bhanu in seat 3. The order is Charu, Esha, Bhanu, Deepak, Asha, and the middle seat holds Bhanu. Shortcut: fix the certain seats, list the placements for the pair, then use the 'not at' clue to cross one out. Trap (A): Esha is second from the left, not in the middle. Trap (C): Deepak would be in the middle only in the rejected arrangement Charu, Esha, Deepak, Asha, Bhanu. Trap (D): stops after seeing two placements for Deepak and Asha, without using the clue about Bhanu.
questions.verify_code:
from itertools import permutations
names = ['Asha', 'Bhanu', 'Charu', 'Deepak', 'Esha']
sols = []
for p in permutations(names):
    if p[0] == 'Charu' and p[1] == 'Esha' and p.index('Deepak') + 1 == p.index('Asha') and p[4] != 'Bhanu':
        sols.append(p)
answer = sols[0][2] if len(sols) == 1 else 'multiple'

questions.question_text: The digits of the number 7524 are rearranged in ascending order to form a new number. Which digit is third from the right in the new number?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ascending order of the digits 7, 5, 2, 4 gives 2, 4, 5, 7, so the new number is 2457. Counting from the right: 7 is first, 5 is second and 4 is third. Shortcut: write the new number down, then count from the stated end. Trap (A): 5 is third from the left, or the answer if the digits are arranged in descending order (7542). Trap (B): 2 is the smallest digit, the first digit of the new number. Trap (D): 7 is the rightmost digit, the first from the right, or the largest digit.
questions.verify_code:
d = sorted([7, 5, 2, 4])
answer = d[-3]

questions.question_text: Find the next number in the series: 2, 5, 4, 8, 6, 11, 8, ?
questions.trap_type: Treated it as a single series
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The terms alternate between two series. Terms 1, 3, 5, 7 are 2, 4, 6, 8 (add 2 each time). Terms 2, 4, 6 are 5, 8, 11 (add 3 each time), so the 8th term is 11 + 3 = 14. Shortcut: if the gaps jump up and down, split the terms into odd and even positions and read each series separately. Trap (B): 10 continues the first series (8 + 2), though the next position belongs to the second. Trap (C): 12 adds 4 to the last term, reading the pattern as a single series. Trap (D): 16 doubles the last term.
questions.verify_code:
even = [5 + 3 * i for i in range(4)]
answer = even[3]

questions.concept_tag: Analogy - letter group shifted by a fixed number of places
questions.question_text: Choose the option that completes the analogy: ACE : GIK :: BDF : ?

options.D: HJL

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In ACE : GIK every letter moves 6 places forward: A to G, C to I, E to K. Apply the same shift to BDF: B to H, D to J, F to L, giving HJL. Shortcut: find the shift from the first letters only (A to G is 6), then apply it to every letter. Trap (A): HJK moves the last letter only 5 places. Trap (B): IKM moves every letter 7 places, from counting A to G as 7. Trap (C): HIJ keeps H but then takes consecutive letters instead of a constant shift.
questions.verify_code:
shift = ord('G') - ord('A')
answer = ''.join(chr(ord(c) + shift) for c in 'BDF')

questions.question_text: In a certain code, every vowel is replaced by a number (A = 1, E = 2, I = 3, O = 4, U = 5) and every consonant stays unchanged. How is the word EDUCATION written in that code?

options.D: 1D2C3T45N

questions.pedagogical_explanation: EDUCATION has the letters E, D, U, C, A, T, I, O, N. The vowels E, U, A, I, O become 2, 5, 1, 3, 4 and the consonants D, C, T, N stay as they are, giving 2D5C1T34N. Shortcut: write the vowel values on a strip, A1 E2 I3 O4 U5, and go letter by letter. Trap (A): 2D5C1T43N swaps the values of I and O. Trap (C): ED5C1T34N leaves the first E uncoded. Trap (D): 1D2C3T45N numbers the vowels in the order they appear in the word instead of using the fixed values.

questions.concept_tag: Seating - four people at the sides of a square table
questions.question_text: Four friends Meena, Rohit, Sana and Tara sit at the four sides of a square table, one on each side, all facing the centre. Meena sits opposite Rohit. Tara sits to the immediate right of Meena. Who sits to the immediate left of Rohit?

options.D: Cannot be determined

questions.trap_type: Left and right seen from the wrong person
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Draw the square and put Meena on the south side facing north and Rohit opposite on the north side facing south. Meena's right hand points east, so Tara is on the east side and Sana is on the west side. Rohit faces south, so his left hand points east, which means the person on his immediate left is Tara. Shortcut: a person facing you has left and right swapped, so redraw the arrows before answering. Trap (B): Sana is what you get by using your own left (west) instead of Rohit's left. Trap (C): Meena sits opposite Rohit, not beside him. Trap (D): treating the position of Sana as unknown, though it is fixed once Meena, Rohit and Tara are placed.
questions.verify_code:
meena = 0
rohit = (meena + 2) % 4
tara = (meena - 1) % 4
sana = ({0, 1, 2, 3} - {meena, rohit, tara}).pop()
who = {meena: 'Meena', rohit: 'Rohit', tara: 'Tara', sana: 'Sana'}
answer = who[(rohit + 1) % 4]

questions.question_text: In a certain code, 'A $ B' means 'A is the father of B' and 'A # B' means 'A is the sister of B'. In the expression P $ Q # R, how is P related to R?

options.D: Father

questions.pedagogical_explanation: P $ Q means P is the father of Q. Q # R means Q is the sister of R, so Q and R are siblings with the same parents. P is therefore the father of R as well. Shortcut: a 'sister' or 'brother' link keeps you in the same generation, so the father of one is the father of the other. Trap (A): Brother reads $ as a sibling link. Trap (B): Uncle treats Q as P's sibling's child rather than P's own child. Trap (C): Grandfather chains the two symbols as two parent steps, adding a generation.

questions.question_text: Find the next number in the series: 2, 6, 7, 21, 22, 66, ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The operations alternate: ×3, +1, ×3, +1, ×3 and so on. 2 × 3 = 6, 6 + 1 = 7, 7 × 3 = 21, 21 + 1 = 22, 22 × 3 = 66, so the next step is 66 + 1 = 67. Shortcut: when terms rise by big jumps and then tiny ones, suspect two alternating operations. Trap (A): 69 adds 3 to the last term. Trap (B): 198 multiplies by 3 again, ignoring the alternation. Trap (D): 68 adds 2, misreading the small step.
questions.verify_code:
x = 2
for i in range(6):
    x = x * 3 if i % 2 == 0 else x + 1
answer = x

questions.concept_tag: Coding-decoding - letters coded as double their position
questions.question_text: In a certain code, every letter is replaced by twice its position in the English alphabet (A = 2, B = 4, C = 6, and so on). How is the word HEAD written in that code?
questions.trap_type: Rule applied to only some letters
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The positions are H = 8, E = 5, A = 1, D = 4. Doubling each gives 16, 10, 2, 8, so HEAD is 16-10-2-8. Shortcut: list the positions first, then double them; A = 1 and D = 4 are quick checks. Trap (A): 8-5-1-4 gives the plain positions without doubling. Trap (C): 16-10-2-4 doubles the first three letters and forgets D. Trap (D): 32-20-4-16 doubles twice.
questions.verify_code:
w = 'HEAD'
out = '-'.join(str(2 * (ord(c) - 64)) for c in w)
opts = {'A': '8-5-1-4', 'B': '16-10-2-8', 'C': '16-10-2-4', 'D': '32-20-4-16'}
answer = next(k for k, v in opts.items() if v == out)

questions.concept_tag: Inequalities - chain and an incomparable pair
questions.question_text:
Statements: K > L ≥ M, N < L
Conclusions:
I. K > N
II. M < N

options.D: Neither I nor II follows

questions.trap_type: Compared two items below the same element
questions.pedagogical_explanation: From K > L and L > N we get K > L > N, so K > N and Conclusion I follows. M and N are both below L (L ≥ M and L > N), but nothing tells us which of the two is smaller, so M < N is not certain and Conclusion II does not follow. Shortcut: build a chain from the statements; two quantities hanging below the same element cannot be compared. Trap (B): picks II by assuming the item with the weaker sign (≥) must be the smaller one. Trap (C): accepts both for the same reason. Trap (D): misses K > N because K > L and N < L point in different directions and the chain through L is not noticed.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some books are not pens. All pens are pencils.
Conclusions:
I. Some books are not pencils.
II. Some pencils are pens.

options.D: Neither I nor II follows

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'All pens are pencils' converts to 'Some pencils are pens', so Conclusion II follows. The books that are not pens could still be pencils, because pencils include more than pens, so 'Some books are not pencils' is not certain and Conclusion I does not follow. Shortcut: convert 'All X are Y' into 'Some Y are X', and remember that a 'not' on the first term never carries over to the next term. Trap (A): picks I alone by thinking 'not a pen' means 'not a pencil'. Trap (B): accepts both for the same reason. Trap (D): rejects II because the statement is written as pens to pencils, not pencils to pens, and misses the conversion.

questions.concept_tag: Direction sense - direction from relative positions
questions.question_text: R is 4 km due east of Q. S is 4 km due south of R. P is 4 km due north of Q. In which direction is S with respect to Q?

options.D: South-east

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take Q as the starting point. R is 4 km east of Q, and S is 4 km south of R, so S is 4 km east and 4 km south of Q, which is exactly south-east. P is a distractor and plays no part. Shortcut: add the east-west and north-south moves separately and combine them. Trap (A): North-east treats 'south of R' as north. Trap (B): South-west flips east into west. Trap (C): North-west uses the position of P (north) and flips east into west.
questions.verify_code:
dx = 4
dy = -4
ns = 'north' if dy > 0 else 'south'
ew = 'east' if dx > 0 else 'west'
answer = ns + '-' + ew

questions.question_text: Choose the option that completes the analogy: Book : Pages :: Wall : ?

options.D: Cement

questions.trap_type: Related thing instead of the part
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A book is made up of pages, so the relation is 'whole : the units it is built from'. A wall is built from bricks. Shortcut: state the relation as a sentence, 'X is made up of Y', and test every option in that sentence. Trap (A): Paint is applied to the surface of a wall, it is not a unit that builds it. Trap (C): Room reverses the relation, since a wall is part of a room. Trap (D): Cement is a binding material used in building, not the units a wall is made of.

questions.concept_tag: Coding-decoding - alternating forward and backward letter shifts
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, PLANT is written as RKCMV. How will MOUSE be written in that code?

options.D: OPWTG

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Compare PLANT with RKCMV letter by letter: P to R (+2), L to K (-1), A to C (+2), N to M (-1), T to V (+2). So letters in odd positions move 2 forward and letters in even positions move 1 back. For MOUSE: M+2 = O, O-1 = N, U+2 = W, S-1 = R, E+2 = G, giving ONWRG. Shortcut: write the shift pattern (+2, -1, +2, -1, +2) under the word before touching any letter. Trap (A): OQWUG moves every letter 2 forward and ignores the back-step on even positions. Trap (B): LQTUD starts the pattern with -1, reversing the order of the two shifts. Trap (D): OPWTG moves the even-position letters 1 forward instead of 1 back, a sign slip.
questions.verify_code:
w = 'MOUSE'
out = ''.join(chr(ord(c) + 2) if i % 2 == 0 else chr(ord(c) - 1) for i, c in enumerate(w))
opts = {'A': 'OQWUG', 'B': 'LQTUD', 'C': 'ONWRG', 'D': 'OPWTG'}
answer = next(k for k, v in opts.items() if v == out)

questions.concept_tag: Number series - gaps that are perfect squares
questions.question_text: Find the next number in the series: 3, 4, 8, 17, 33, ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The gaps between the terms are 1, 4, 9, 16, the squares of 1, 2, 3, 4, so the next gap is 5² = 25 and the next term is 33 + 25 = 58. Shortcut: when the gaps grow faster each time, write the gaps and then the gaps of the gaps (3, 5, 7); a pattern of perfect squares shows up. Trap (B): 49 repeats the last gap of 16. Trap (C): 56 freezes the second difference at 7, giving a gap of 23. Trap (D): 53 guesses that the gaps grow by a flat 4 (16 + 4), though the increases 3, 5, 7 are not constant.
questions.verify_code:
x = 3
for n in range(1, 6):
    x = x + n * n
answer = x

questions.concept_tag: Analogy - number pairs with a cube-based rule
questions.question_text: In the pairs 2 : 9 and 3 : 28, the second number is obtained from the first by the same rule. Which number will pair with 5 in the same way?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Test the rule on both given pairs: 2³ + 1 = 9 and 3³ + 1 = 28, so the second number is the cube of the first plus 1. For 5: 5³ + 1 = 126. Shortcut: 9 and 28 sit just above the cubes 8 and 27, so test 'cube plus a constant' first. Trap (A): 26 is 5² + 1, carried over from the familiar 'square plus one' pattern; it fails on the pair 2 : 9 (2² + 1 = 5). Trap (B): 125 is 5³ with the +1 forgotten. Trap (C): 124 is 5³ - 1, with the sign of the constant flipped.
questions.verify_code:
rule_ok = (2 ** 3 + 1 == 9) and (3 ** 3 + 1 == 28)
answer = 5 ** 3 + 1 if rule_ok else 0

questions.concept_tag: Blood relations - a clue that loops back to the parent
questions.question_text: Pointing to a girl, Sumit says, 'She is the daughter of my father's only sister's only brother.' How is the girl related to Sumit?

options.D: Paternal aunt

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Work from the inside out. 'My father's only sister' is Sumit's paternal aunt. Her only brother must be Sumit's father, because he is her brother and she has no other. So the girl is the daughter of Sumit's father, which makes her Sumit's sister. Shortcut: when a clue loops back through 'only sister's only brother', it returns to the starting person's parent, so resolve that loop first. Trap (A): Cousin stops at 'father's sister' and treats the girl as that aunt's child. Trap (C): Niece treats the girl as the child of one of Sumit's brothers or sisters. Trap (D): Paternal aunt confuses the girl with the father's sister mentioned inside the clue.

questions.question_text: P is the mother of Q. Q is the sister of R. R is the father of S. T is the brother of P. How is T related to S?

options.D: Cousin

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Q is R's sister, so both Q and R are P's children. R is the father of S, so P is S's paternal grandmother. T is P's brother, so T is S's grandmother's brother, a great-uncle. Shortcut: sort everyone into generations: P and T (first), Q and R (second), S (third). T is two generations above S and is a sibling of P, not a parent. Trap (A): Uncle places T one generation too low, as if he were R's brother. Trap (C): Grandfather treats T as P's husband instead of her brother. Trap (D): Cousin places T in S's own generation.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All locks are keys. Some keys are chains.
Conclusions:
I. Some locks are chains.
II. No lock is a chain.

options.D: Neither I nor II follows

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'All locks are keys' and 'Some keys are chains' share the middle term 'keys', but the chain-keys need not be the keys that are locks. So no direct link between locks and chains is forced, and neither 'Some locks are chains' nor 'No lock is a chain' follows on its own. Yet exactly one of the two must be true, because they are a complementary some/no pair on the same two terms. So either I or II follows. Shortcut: if the conclusions are a 'some' and a 'no' (or 'some not') pair on the same terms and neither follows alone, the answer is 'Either I or II'. Trap (B): Both would need two contradictory statements to be true together. Trap (C): Only I assumes the chain-keys include locks, which the statements never say. Trap (D): Neither stops after finding that neither follows alone and misses the either-or rule.

questions.concept_tag: Syllogism - carrying a 'some' group through a chain
questions.question_text:
Statements: Some tables are chairs. All chairs are benches. No bench is a stool.
Conclusions:
I. Some tables are benches.
II. Some tables are not stools.

options.D: Neither I nor II follows

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Some tables are chairs, and all chairs are benches, so those tables are benches: Conclusion I follows. No bench is a stool, so those same tables are not stools, which gives 'Some tables are not stools': Conclusion II follows. Shortcut: pick out the 'some' group (the tables that are chairs) and carry it through every later statement. Trap (A): Only I misses that 'No bench is a stool' passes on to the tables through the chairs. Trap (B): Only II sees the 'not stools' link but misses the simpler 'All chairs are benches' step. Trap (D): Neither assumes that a 'some' statement cannot be carried on through an 'all' statement.

questions.concept_tag: Direction sense - positions of five points
questions.question_text: Point A is 5 km north of point B. Point C is 5 km east of B. Point D is 5 km south of C, and point E is 5 km west of D. How far and in which direction is E from A?

options.D: 10 km south

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take B as the origin. Then A = (0, 5), C = (5, 0), D = (5, -5) and E = (0, -5). E lies directly below A, 10 km away, so E is 10 km south of A. Shortcut: track the north-south and east-west changes separately; the 5 km east and 5 km west cancel completely. Trap (A): 10 km north has the right distance but reverses the direction. Trap (B): 5 km south compares E with B instead of with A. Trap (C): 15 km south adds three of the 5 km legs without separating the north-south moves from the east-west moves.
questions.verify_code:
pos = {'B': (0, 0)}
pos['A'] = (0, 5)
pos['C'] = (5, 0)
pos['D'] = (5, -5)
pos['E'] = (0, -5)
dx = pos['E'][0] - pos['A'][0]
dy = pos['E'][1] - pos['A'][1]
dist = abs(dx) + abs(dy)
direction = 'south' if dy < 0 else 'north'
opts = {'A': (10, 'north'), 'B': (5, 'south'), 'C': (15, 'south'), 'D': (10, 'south')}
answer = next(k for k, v in opts.items() if v == (dist, direction))

questions.concept_tag: Series - letter pairs with growing shifts in opposite directions
questions.question_text: Find the next term in the series: AZ, CX, FU, JQ, ?

options.D: OL

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The first letters move +2, +3, +4 (A to C, C to F, F to J) and the second letters move -2, -3, -4 (Z to X, X to U, U to Q). The next shifts are +5 and -5: J to O and Q to L, giving OL. Shortcut: treat the two letters as two separate series and write each gap beneath it. Trap (A): NM keeps the last shifts of +4 and -4 instead of growing them. Trap (B): OM extends the first letter correctly (+5) but forgets to extend the gap of the second letter (-4). Trap (C): PK over-extends both shifts to 6.
questions.verify_code:
a = 1
z = 26
for g in range(2, 6):
    a = a + g
    z = z - g
answer = chr(64 + a) + chr(64 + z)

questions.concept_tag: Coding-decoding - reversal followed by a vowel change
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, a word is first written backwards and then every vowel in it is replaced by the next letter of the alphabet (A by B, E by F, I by J, and so on). How will STREAM be written in that code?

options.D: MBERTS

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step 1: write STREAM backwards to get MAERTS. Step 2: change each vowel to the next letter: A becomes B and E becomes F, giving MBFRTS. Shortcut: do the two steps one at a time and write the intermediate word, so no step can be skipped. Trap (A): STRFBM changes the vowels but forgets to reverse the word. Trap (B): MAERTS reverses the word but forgets to change the vowels. Trap (D): MBERTS changes only the first vowel A to B and leaves E unchanged.
questions.verify_code:
w = 'STREAM'[::-1]
out = ''.join(chr(ord(c) + 1) if c in 'AEIOU' else c for c in w)
opts = {'A': 'STRFBM', 'B': 'MAERTS', 'C': 'MBFRTS', 'D': 'MBERTS'}
answer = next(k for k, v in opts.items() if v == out)

questions.question_text: Find the next number in the series: 7, 9, 13, 21, 37, ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The gaps are 2, 4, 8, 16, doubling each time, so the next gap is 32 and the next term is 37 + 32 = 69. (Equivalently, each term is 2 × previous - 5.) Shortcut: write the gaps first; if they double, the series is 'previous term + 2ⁿ'. Trap (B): 53 repeats the last gap of 16. Trap (C): 74 doubles the last term instead of the last gap. Trap (D): 61 adds the last increase in the gaps (8) to the last gap (16), giving 24, as if the gaps grew by a fixed amount.
questions.verify_code:
seq = [7]
g = 2
for i in range(5):
    seq.append(seq[-1] + g)
    g = g * 2
answer = seq[-1]

questions.concept_tag: Number series - squares of prime numbers
questions.question_text: Find the next number in the series: 4, 9, 25, 49, 121, ?
questions.trap_type: Next integer taken instead of next prime
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The terms are 2², 3², 5², 7², 11², the squares of consecutive prime numbers. The next prime after 11 is 13, so the next term is 13² = 169. Shortcut: when every term is a perfect square, take the square roots first (2, 3, 5, 7, 11) and read that list. Trap (A): 144 is 12², using the next integer instead of the next prime. Trap (C): 196 is 14², continuing the roots with a gap of 3 (11 + 3). Trap (D): 289 is 17², skipping 13 by jumping to the prime after it.
questions.verify_code:
primes = [n for n in range(2, 20) if all(n % d for d in range(2, n))]
seq = [p * p for p in primes[:6]]
answer = seq[-1]

questions.concept_tag: Analogy - instrument and the quantity it measures
questions.question_text: Choose the option that completes the analogy: Thermometer : Temperature :: Barometer : ?

options.D: Rainfall

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A thermometer is the instrument that measures temperature. A barometer is the instrument that measures atmospheric pressure. Shortcut: state the relation as the sentence 'X measures Y' and test each option in it; every wrong option is measured by a different instrument. Trap (A): Wind speed is measured by an anemometer. Trap (B): Humidity is measured by a hygrometer. Trap (D): Rainfall is measured by a rain gauge.

questions.concept_tag: Analogy - letter words and the product of their positions
questions.question_text: Find the number that completes the analogy: BED : 40 :: HOT : ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In BED, B = 2, E = 5 and D = 4, and 2 × 5 × 4 = 40, so each word stands for the product of the alphabet positions of its letters. For HOT: H = 8, O = 15, T = 20, and 8 × 15 × 20 = 2,400. Shortcut: test the sum first (2 + 5 + 4 = 11, not 40) and then the product (40); only the product fits. Trap (A): 43 is the sum of the positions (8 + 15 + 20). Trap (B): 160 multiplies only the first and last letters (8 × 20). Trap (C): 120 multiplies only the first two letters (8 × 15).
questions.verify_code:
rule_ok = (ord('B') - 64) * (ord('E') - 64) * (ord('D') - 64) == 40
answer = (ord('H') - 64) * (ord('O') - 64) * (ord('T') - 64) if rule_ok else 0

questions.concept_tag: Inequalities - strict and non-strict links in a chain
questions.question_text:
Statements: W < X ≤ Y = Z
Conclusions:
I. W < Z
II. X < Z

options.D: Neither I nor II follows

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In the chain W < X ≤ Y = Z, the link W < X is strict, so the whole comparison from W to Z is strict: W < Z, and Conclusion I follows. For X and Z the chain is X ≤ Y = Z, which gives only X ≤ Z; X could equal Z, so X < Z is not certain and Conclusion II does not follow. Shortcut: a chain is strict only if at least one link in the stretch you are using is strict. Trap (B): Only II reads ≤ as <. Trap (C): Both follow repeats the same slip for Conclusion II. Trap (D): Neither doubts Conclusion I because the chain contains a ≤, forgetting that one strict link makes the whole stretch strict.

questions.concept_tag: Seating - row arrangement with an 'exactly two between' clue
questions.question_text: Six friends Arun, Bela, Chirag, Dhruv, Esha and Farah sit in a row facing north. Arun sits at the right end. Exactly two persons sit between Arun and Bela. Chirag sits immediately to the right of Bela. Dhruv sits next to Arun. Esha sits somewhere to the left of Farah. Who sits second from the left end?

options.D: Chirag

questions.trap_type: Seats counted from the wrong end

Statements: All taps are pipes. Some pipes are pumps. All pumps are valves.

I. Some pipes are valves.
II. Some taps are valves.

options.D: Neither I nor II follows

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Some pipes are pumps, and all pumps are valves, so those pipes are valves: Conclusion I follows. Taps are only a part of the pipes, and the statements never say that any tap is a pump, so the pipes that are pumps may include no taps at all; Conclusion II does not follow. options.D: Meera

Trap (A): Nisha sits on Jaya's immediate right, so this answer swaps left and right. Trap (B): Leena sits second to Jaya's left, not immediately to her left. Trap (C): Ishan sits second to Jaya's right.

questions.concept_tag: Blood relations - child of a mother's brother

options.D: Maternal uncle
